sec.title: Background
sec.p: Early deep prostate‐specific antigen (PSA) decline after the initiation of androgen receptor signaling inhibitor (ARSI) therapy is associated with favorable long‐term outcomes in metastatic castration‐sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC). The Nadir ARSI‐Derived Integrative Response (NADIR) model was recently developed using Phase III trial data to predict the probability of achieving a favorable early PSA response. However, its performance in real‐world clinical settings remains unclear.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We retrospectively reviewed 196 patients with mCSPC who received first‐line ARSI therapy at Hiroshima University Hospital and affiliated institutions between 2018 and 2025; 186 had complete data required to calculate the NADIR score. An early favorable PSA response was defined as a decline in PSA to ≤ 0.2 ng/mL within 6 months of treatment initiation. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and calibration was evaluated using calibration plots. Patients were stratified into tertiles based on the NADIR score, and time‐to‐event outcomes, including overall survival (OS) and time to castration‐resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), were analyzed using the Kaplan–Meier method.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The proportion of patients with an early favorable PSA response decreased stepwise across the upper, middle, and lower tertiles (61.3%, 33.8%, and 17.7%, respectively; Cochran–Armitage trend test, p < 0.01). The NADIR model demonstrated acceptable discrimination for predicting an early favorable PSA response, with an AUC of 0.74 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.66–0.81). Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes was maintained across NADIR‐defined risk groups. In a univariable analysis treating the NADIR score as a continuous variable, higher NADIR scores were strongly associated with an early favorable PSA response (odds ratio per 10% increase, 1.74; 95% CI 1.36–2.23; p < 0.001). CRPC‐free survival differed significantly across NADIR‐defined tertiles, whereas OS did not differ significantly.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this real‐world cohort, the NADIR model retained acceptable predictive performance, suggesting applicability in routine clinical practice and potential utility in individualized pretreatment clinical management.
Keywords: calibration, castration‐resistant prostate cancer, discrimination, predictive model, prostate‐specific antigen, treatment intensification

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Prostate cancer (PC) remains one of the most common malignancies in men worldwide. In 2022, approximately 1,400,000 new cases were reported globally [1]. Among patients with PC, approximately 5%–10% present with metastatic castration‐sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC) at the initial diagnosis [2]. Treatment for mCSPC has improved substantially over the past decade. Beyond androgen deprivation therapy alone, multiple Phase III trials have demonstrated consistent overall survival (OS) benefits with treatment intensification, including docetaxel and several androgen receptor signaling inhibitors (ARSIs) such as abiraterone, apalutamide, enzalutamide, and darolutamide [3, 4]. With an expanding set of highly effective regimens (doublet and triplet combinations), clinicians must increasingly decide on the appropriate intensity and timing of therapy for individual patients.

Early prostate‐specific antigen (PSA) responses serve as a clinically accessible marker of treatment sensitivity and tumor biology. Deep PSA suppression, particularly reaching PSA < 0.2 ng/mL at 6 months, has been associated with favorable long‐term outcomes in mCSPC, including in long‐term analyses of randomized trial populations [5]. In addition, several studies have consistently shown that both PSA nadir after androgen deprivation therapy and time to PSA nadir are prognostic factors for subsequent disease progression and survival [6, 7]. Collectively, these data support the clinical plausibility of “favorable PSA response by 6 months” as an early marker of biological aggressiveness and endocrine sensitivity. Accordingly, numerous prognostic models based on baseline clinical characteristics and post‐treatment PSA nadir have been described in the relevant literature [3, 6, 7, 8]. However, there is no established model for quantitatively predicting an early favorable PSA response at the time of ARSI initiation.

Recently, Roy and colleagues developed and validated the Nadir ARSI‐Derived Integrative Response (NADIR) model using data from Phase III clinical trials. This multivariable tool estimates the probability of achieving PSA ≤ 0.2 ng/mL by 6 months based on pretreatment clinical and laboratory parameters in mCSPC patients initiating ARSI‐based therapy [9]. However, prediction models derived from Phase III trial data sets may not transport directly to routine practice, where case‐mix, comorbidities, measurement variability, and treatment selection are more heterogeneous. Therefore, we evaluated the performance of the previously reported NADIR model by applying it to real‐world data derived from Hiroshima University‐affiliated institutions.

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: This study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines for clinical research reporting in the field of urology [10, 11, 12].

sec.title: Hiroshima Cohort
sec.p: We retrospectively reviewed 196 patients with mCSPC who received first‐line systemic therapy with an ARSI at Hiroshima University Hospital and affiliated institutions between 2018 and 2025. All patients had pathologically confirmed adenocarcinoma of the prostate. Clinical information was retrospectively collected from the medical records. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Hiroshima University (Authorization Number: E2021‐2519) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The requirement of informed consent was waived owing to the retrospective nature of the study. Patient data were managed using the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) system hosted by Hiroshima University [13, 14], as previously described [15, 16, 17].

sec.title: Exposures and Variable Definitions
sec.p: The NADIR model was previously developed using a large, multicenter training cohort and subsequently validated in independent internal and external cohorts [9]. Briefly, the model was constructed using multivariable logistic regression to predict the likelihood of achieving a favorable early PSA response, defined as a decline in PSA to ≤ 0.2 ng/mL within 6 months of ARSI therapy. Continuous variables, including age, body mass index, and hemoglobin level, were log‐transformed, and baseline PSA was modeled using restricted cubic splines with four degrees of freedom to account for nonlinear effects. In the original model development, a variable importance analysis showed that baseline PSA level, hemoglobin level, metastatic volume as defined by the Chemohormonal Therapy Versus Androgen Ablation Randomized Trial for Extensive Disease in Prostate Cancer (CHAARTED) criteria, age at diagnosis, body mass index, presence of visceral metastasis, and metastatic stage at presentation (synchronous vs. metachronous) contributed significantly to the predictive performance of the full model (Table S1). All patients in the Hiroshima cohort had metastatic disease at the initial diagnosis. Therefore, all cases were classified as having synchronous metastatic presentation. Details of model development, validation procedures, and performance metrics are described in the original publication and on the publicly available model website (https://bit.ly/42Ec1lP). The NADIR model was applied without recalibration or modification, and predicted probabilities were obtained using the publicly available model implementation. Among the 196 patients in the Hiroshima cohort, 186 had complete data for all variables required to calculate the NADIR model. As an exploratory analysis, patients were stratified into tertiles (upper, middle, and lower) based on the NADIR score.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary endpoint was early favorable PSA response, defined as a decline in PSA to ≤ 0.2 ng/mL within 6 months of treatment initiation. The secondary efficacy endpoints were OS and time to castration‐resistant prostate cancer (CRPC). OS was defined as the time from the initiation of treatment, which served as the index date, to death from any cause. Time to CRPC was defined as the interval from treatment initiation to the development of CRPC, as determined based on clinical information and laboratory findings documented in medical records. CRPC was defined according to standard criteria, including biochemical progression, defined as a ≥ 25% increase from the PSA nadir with an absolute increase of ≥ 2 ng/mL, confirmed by a second value, and/or radiographic progression, despite castration levels of testosterone (< 50 ng/dL). Patients who did not experience the event of interest were censored at the date of the last clinical visit or the last confirmed date of survival.

sec.title: Statistical Analyses
sec.p: Baseline characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Continuous variables are reported as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs) and were compared across NADIR tertiles using the Kruskal–Wallis test. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages and were compared using the χ 2 test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. When pairwise comparisons were reported, the upper tertile was prespecified as the reference group (upper vs. middle and upper vs. lower), and p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm–Bonferroni method. Trends in the proportion of early favorable PSA response across NADIR‐defined tertiles were assessed using the Cochran–Armitage trend test. Model discrimination was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) calculated using DeLong's method. Baseline PSA was log‐transformed to account for its skewed distribution prior to analysis. Calibration was evaluated visually using a decile‐based calibration plot comparing predicted probabilities with observed event rates. Time‐to‐event outcomes were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method; overall differences among tertiles were assessed using a global log‐rank test, followed by prespecified pairwise log‐rank comparisons using the upper tertile as the reference with Holm–Bonferroni adjustment. All tests were two‐sided, and p values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed using R (ver. 4.3.0, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

sec.title: Baseline Patient Characteristics
sec.p: Baseline patient characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The median follow‐up time was 22.8 months (IQR, 14.7–38.9), and 48 deaths were observed. All 186 patients were stratified into tertiles based on the NADIR model. Overall, background characteristics such as age and body mass index did not differ substantially across the tertiles. In contrast, variables incorporated into the NADIR model, including baseline PSA, metastatic volume, and hemoglobin level, showed systematic differences in their distributions according to the NADIR score stratification. Baseline PSA levels differed significantly among the tertiles, with higher values observed in the lower tertile. In addition, the distribution of high‐volume disease differed significantly, with a higher proportion of high‐volume disease in the lower tertile. Furthermore, hemoglobin levels at diagnosis differed significantly among the tertiles, with lower levels observed in the lower tertile.

sec.title: Early Favorable PSA Response
sec.p: A significant trend was observed in the proportion of early favorable PSA responses across the three NADIR model‐defined tertiles. The proportion of early favorable PSA response was highest in the upper tertile (61.3%), followed by the middle tertile (33.8%), and lowest in the lower tertile (17.7%) (Figure 1). This monotonic trend was statistically significant (Cochran–Armitage trend test, p < 0.001), indicating a clear gradient in early PSA response according to NADIR‐based risk stratification. Consistently, in the univariable analysis treating the NADIR score as a continuous variable, higher NADIR scores were strongly associated with an early favorable PSA response. For every 10% increase in the NADIR score, the odds of achieving an early favorable PSA response increased by 74% (odds ratio [OR], 1.74; 95% CI, 1.36–2.23; p < 0.001).

sec.title: Discrimination and Calibration of the NADIR Model
sec.p: The NADIR model demonstrated good discrimination for predicting an early favorable PSA response. The receiver operating characteristic analysis yielded an AUC of 0.74 (95% CI 0.66–0.81), indicating acceptable to good discriminatory performance (Figure 2A). In comparison, the AUC of baseline PSA alone was 0.66 (95% CI 0.58–0.74), which was lower than that of the NADIR model. These results suggest that the NADIR model provides improved predictive performance over baseline PSA alone. In addition, the calibration analysis showed good agreement between predicted probabilities and observed event rates across the range of risk. In decile‐based calibration plots, the observed proportions of early favorable PSA response closely followed the ideal 45° line, with no substantial evidence of systematic overestimation or underestimation (Figure 2B). The Brier score was 0.209, indicating acceptable overall model performance. These findings indicate that the NADIR model is not only discriminative but also well calibrated for early PSA response in this cohort.

sec.title: Association of NADIR Model‐Defined Tertiles With Time‐to‐Event Outcomes
sec.p: Next, patients were stratified into tertiles according to the NADIR model, and OS and time to CRPC were evaluated using the Kaplan–Meier method. For time to CRPC, a statistically significant separation of the survival curves was observed across NADIR model‐defined tertiles, with patients in the upper tertile demonstrating longer CRPC‐free survival in comparison to those in the middle and lower tertiles (Figure 3A). In contrast, for OS, Kaplan–Meier analyses showed no statistically significant differences among NADIR model‐defined tertiles, although a trend toward more favorable survival was observed in the upper tertile (Figure 3B).

caption.p: Association between NADIR model‐defined tertiles and time‐to‐event outcomes. (A) Time to CRPC. (B) Overall survival. NADIR, Nadir ARSI‐Derived Integrative Response; CRPC, castration‐resistant prostate cancer. [Color figure can be viewed at wileyonlinelibrary.com]

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we evaluated the performance of the previously reported NADIR model using real‐world clinical data from Hiroshima University Hospital and affiliated institutions. The model demonstrated acceptable discrimination for predicting an early favorable PSA response (AUC, 0.74). This predictive performance was comparable to that reported by Roy and colleagues in the original Phase III trial‐based development and validation cohorts (AUC, 0.76 for internal validation and 0.82 for external validation). In addition, the overall calibration between the predicted probabilities and observed clinical outcomes was well preserved across NADIR model‐defined risk groups. These findings suggest that the NADIR model may be applicable as a predictive tool for estimating the likelihood of achieving an early favorable PSA response in heterogeneous real‐world clinical settings. In addition, the NADIR model demonstrated improved predictive performance compared with baseline PSA alone, as reflected by a higher AUC. This finding suggests that integrating multiple clinical variables provides incremental predictive value beyond a single biomarker.

Beyond predicting an early favorable PSA response, the NADIR model also provided clinically interpretable prognostic stratification. CRPC‐free survival was separated across NADIR model‐defined tertiles, consistent with previous reports that early deep PSA decline and PSA nadir kinetics are linked to long‐term outcomes [5, 6, 7]. OS did not differ significantly among the NADIR model‐defined tertiles. This may be attributable to the limited sample size in a single‐region real‐world cohort, the possibility of insufficient follow‐up, and the heterogeneity of post‐progression therapies.

In mCSPC patients receiving ARSI therapy, longitudinal assessment of PSA levels is fundamental for evaluating treatment response. However, in patients with insufficient early responses, therapeutic resistance may already be emerging, and delayed intervention may attenuate the potential benefit of subsequent treatment modifications [18]. From this perspective, deferring treatment reassessment until 6 months after treatment initiation based solely on whether a favorable early PSA response has been achieved may delay optimal therapeutic intervention. Therefore, the identification, at the time of diagnosis, of patients who are unlikely to achieve a favorable early PSA response may help guide intensified monitoring and, when clinically appropriate, earlier re‐evaluation of the treatment strategy. Given the increasing focus on upfront combination therapy rather than sequential treatment intensification, this model may serve as a supportive tool to facilitate individualized pretreatment clinical management, rather than replacing existing clinical decision‐making frameworks.

This study had several limitations. First, given its retrospective design and reliance on routinely collected clinical data, variability in assessments, residual confounding, and treatment selection bias cannot be fully excluded. Second, the analyses were restricted to patients with complete data required to calculate the NADIR score, which may have introduced selection bias if data missingness was not random. Third, all patients in the Hiroshima cohort had synchronous metastatic disease at diagnosis. Therefore, the applicability of the NADIR model to patients with metachronous metastatic presentation remains uncertain. Fourth, the objective of this study was to evaluate the discriminative performance and applicability of the previously reported NADIR model using real‐world clinical data. Therefore, we did not perform analyses aimed at constructing a new multivariable prognostic model or at directly comparing the NADIR model with conventional risk stratification systems. Fifth, different ARSIs were used in this cohort, and treatment‐related heterogeneity may have influenced PSA response. However, the NADIR model was originally developed using data from multiple Phase III trials that included different ARSIs, supporting its applicability across treatment types. Sixth, the use of a fixed 6‐month PSA threshold may not fully capture variability in PSA kinetics among individual patients. Therefore, future prospective studies with standardized data collection, including both synchronous and metachronous cases, are warranted to further confirm the reproducibility and clinical utility of the NADIR model.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study suggests that the NADIR model can predict a favorable PSA response based on real‐world data. These findings indicate that the model may be applicable beyond clinical trial populations and support its use in routine clinical practice.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The Hiroshima cohort contains patient‐level clinical information from Hiroshima University Hospital and affiliated institutions and cannot be made publicly available due to privacy considerations. De‐identified aggregate data and the analysis code are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request and subject to institutional data‐sharing policies.
